title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in the earlier part of E510, and in the companion paper E509, Euler derived a linearized equilibrium equation for a vertical column loaded only by its own weight (weight q per unit length, flexural rigidity EI). In that derivation the top A is free and the abscissa x is measured downward from A. The bending moment at x is the sum of q(y(s) - y(x)) over the part above x, which gives EI y''' + q x y' = 0. In modern form y'(x) = sqrt(x) J_{-1/3}((2/3) sqrt(q/EI) x^{3/2}), up to a constant. This 'curva mirabilis' oscillates without end: it has infinitely many extrema of y (vertical tangents) and infinitely many inflection points. The previous page states the paradox. Read naively, the equation seems not to bound the height, yet Euler insists that for every strength there is a limiting height. His resolution starts here.

§3: Euler replaces the column, at least in thought, by an elastic lamina 'of the same strength'. The lamina resists bending exactly as much as the column resists fracture; the only difference is that the lamina actually bends while the column breaks. Such a lamina, under its own weight alone, can be bent into exactly the curve derived earlier, provided all ordinates XY are treated as infinitely small. The figure exaggerates them only for visibility. This is the linearization: the shape is an eigenfunction fixed only up to scale, so the ordinates keep constant ratios to one another. The abscissae stretch in proportion to stiffness. Implicitly the length scale is (EI/q)^{1/3}.

§4: Any arc AY of the curve is an equilibrium shape of a lamina of length AY whose end Y is held firmly in the direction of the tangent at Y (a clamp, generally oblique). The special points are those where the ordinates are maximal or minimal, i.e. where the tangent is vertical (y' = 0). If such a point is taken as the lower end, and the lamina is set vertically into the floor (a vertical clamp), then the part above takes the drawn shape under its own weight and stays in equilibrium.

In modern terms these are exactly the clamped-base / free-top self-weight buckling configurations. They occur where J_{-1/3}((2/3) sqrt(q/EI) L^{3/2}) = 0. The first zero (about 1.866) gives L ≈ 1.986 (EI/q)^{1/3}, i.e. qL^3/EI ≈ 7.84. This is the critical height usually credited to Greenhill (1881); the later zeros give the higher modes.

§5, on the next page, treats inflection points (zero moment) as bases on which the lamina merely stands. Euler notes the centre of gravity lies vertically above that point and the equilibrium is labile. §6 then rejects all these free-top cases for his actual question, in which both ends stay on one vertical. He therefore adds a horizontal force at the top.
errors: Physically, identifying fracture strength with flexural rigidity ('lamina quae inflexioni tantum reluctetur, quantum columna fractioni resistit') conflates strength and stiffness. Euler uses this analogy consistently in his column papers, but it is a conceptual, not mathematical, gap.
The analysis is purely linear (ordinates infinitesimal), so amplitude is undetermined. Euler states this correctly; it is a limitation, not an error.

Arguably an interpretive misjudgment rather than a calculational error. By dismissing the free-top cases as irrelevant to his question, Euler does not draw the conclusion that the first vertical-tangent point already gives the critical height of a flagpole-type column (clamped base, free top) under self-weight.

ideas.what: Replacing a column by an elastic lamina of equivalent 'strength' to study collapse under load
ideas.modern_name: elastic buckling model of columns (Euler-Bernoulli beam stability)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 Additamentum de curvis elasticis; 1757/1759 'Sur la force des colonnes')

ideas.what: Ordinates treated as infinitely small, shape fixed only up to ratios
ideas.modern_name: linearized eigenvalue problem; buckling mode determined up to scale

ideas.what: Height scale grows with stiffness while ordinate ratios stay fixed
ideas.usually_credited_to: implicit in Euler; explicit in Greenhill 1881

ideas.what: Any arc of the solution curve, clamped at its lower end along its tangent, is an equilibrium shape; vertical-tangent points correspond to a vertically clamped base
ideas.modern_name: clamped-free self-weight buckling modes (zeros of J_{-1/3}); Greenhill's problem
ideas.usually_credited_to: A. G. Greenhill (1881) for the critical height qL^3/EI ≈ 7.837
ideas.where_published: E510 (this page) and E509, as a qualitative statement; the numerical root is not given here

missed.claim: Euler explicitly says that the points of the free-top self-weight curve with vertical tangents serve as vertically clamped bases. Such a lamina, of length from A to that point, stands in (neutral) equilibrium bent under its own weight. These are precisely the eigen-lengths of the clamped-free self-weight column, so the first such point is Greenhill's critical height (qL^3/EI ≈ 7.84). Euler had the equation, its series solution and this interpretation in 1778. He set it aside as irrelevant only because he wanted both ends on one vertical. Standard engineering histories (e.g. Timoshenko) say Euler failed at self-weight buckling and credit Greenhill. Truesdell's 1960 account may already note the near-miss; I am unsure.
missed.quote: Quod si ergo quodpiam horum punctorum pro infimo termino laminae elasticae accipiatur, is pauimento quoque verticaliter infigi debebit, vt de hoc situ declinare nequeat; tum enim pars superior figuram assignatam ob proprium pondus recipere simulque in aequilibrio consistere poterit.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Priority and history: the clamped-free self-weight buckling problem (the 'flagpole' or tall-tree problem) is conceptually solved here, including the higher modes. Only the numerical first zero of the series is missing. The credit usually goes entirely to Greenhill.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is mostly interpretive set-up. It does, however, contain an explicit statement that amounts to the Greenhill clamped-free self-weight buckling configuration, which Euler discards. Specialists such as Truesdell probably know Euler came close, so this is a moderate rather than a striking finding.
transcription_corrections: 'ad eo maiorem altitudinem' is as printed (ad eo = to a greater height in proportion); no change needed.
Transcription otherwise matches the image; the margin note 'Tab. IV. Fig. 2.' sits beside 'vbicunque libuerit, accipere licet'.
